title: Watch and pray (Luke 21:29–38)
hook: don't let your hearts be weighed down with cares; watch and pray

segments.voice: Yesterday, lift up your heads. Your line was your redemption draws near. When bad news bent your head, did you look up? Day five hundred seventy-six.

It's eleven at night. The day is over, but your mind isn't. The email you didn't answer. The bill. The thing your sister said. You lie down, and your heart feels like a backpack someone forgot to take off. You've been carrying it all day, and you're carrying it into sleep. Jesus has just finished his hard words about the end, wars and signs and the sky shaking. And the way he closes isn't with more alarm. It's with a fig tree, and then a warning that sounds as if he'd seen your eleven o'clock.

First the tree. When the fig tree and all the trees put out their leaves, you know summer is near. Nobody needs a calendar. You just look. Then a sentence Christians have leaned on for centuries: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away." And then the warning, in the King James words: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares." Overcharged. The Greek word means weighed down, made heavy. Look at the three things on the list. Surfeiting, which means too much of a good thing, eating and drinking past the point of joy. Drunkenness. And cares of this life. Ordinary worries. He puts worry on the same list as a hangover: both leave the heart too heavy to notice what's coming. Then the cure: "Watch ye therefore, and pray always." The Greek for watch here means to stay awake, to keep from sleep, like a guard on night duty. Not anxious. Alert. Luke ends the chapter with Jesus living it out. By day he teaches in the temple. Every night he goes out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives. And early every morning, the people come to the temple to hear him. Watch and pray is not a slogan for a crisis. It's a rhythm: carry the day lightly enough that you can still see the leaves.
screen: then, large: `WATCH YE THEREFORE, AND PRAY ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one care before sleep. You can do a small version now. Settle, and breathe. Notice what's sitting heaviest on you today. Name it, plainly, in a few words. Now imagine it's an actual weight in your hands. You're not solving it. You're just setting it down, for tonight, on the floor beside the bed. It'll still be there in the morning if you need it. If you pray, you can hand it to God by name. Tonight, before you sleep, do it again with whatever is heaviest then. The bell holds the time.
Watch and pray. Jesus's last instruction in his teaching about the end: stay awake, don't let cares weigh your heart down, and keep praying.
Your line: watch and pray. Tonight, before you sleep, name one care out loud and set it down beside the bed until morning. Day five hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Many Christians keep evening prayer, such as Compline, to hand over the day before sleep, and the call to watch and pray shapes the season of Advent in many churches.

fork.setup: Jesus has warned of hard days ahead. what does he say is most likely to make people miss the day when it comes?
options: not studying the signs closely enough.
hearts weighed down with excess and the cares of this life.
fork.reveal: "lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life." ordinary heaviness, not a lack of information.

original.note: Greek: stay awake, keep from sleeping. the word Luke uses for 'watch' in 21:36.

trapdoor: what you thought: be on high alert for the end of the world.
what it means: don't let excess or worry make your heart so heavy you can't see what God is doing; stay awake and keep praying.
what a scholar hears: 'overcharged' renders a Greek verb for weighing down, and 'watch' is agrypneo, to go without sleep, the language of a sentry.

sources.quoted: Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away.
Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.
Watch ye therefore, and pray always

notes: 'Overcharged' renders a form of the Greek bareo, to weigh down; 'watch' renders agrypneo, to be sleepless. Confirm.
Luke 21:37 says he 'abode in the mount that is called the mount of Olives'; the script says he went out to spend the night there; the Greek verb can mean to lodge in the open. Confirm.
Original-language form ἀγρυπνεῖτε (present imperative plural) as in Luke 21:36. Confirm accent and form.
